title: The politics of whether we need more or less ‘gifted and talented’ education
summary: Who can argue against gifted and talented education? In a time of limited resources and inequitable access, maybe we should try, writes Kalman Hettleman. But he also says that, despite challenges, now is not the time to abandon GTE, but to reform it.
content:
by Kalman Hettleman, Maryland Matters November 25, 2025

by Kalman Hettleman, Maryland Matters November 25, 2025

What could be wrong with public schools providing instruction tailored to fulfill the potential of “gifted and talented” students (GTE)? Our nation has a vital interest in gifted and talented citizens and workers.

The National Association for Gifted Children states that education for gifted and talented students must move students “at an educational pace matching their abilities and readiness for advanced curriculum rather than restricting them to a set of grade-level standards based on their age.”

That’s the persuasive case for more GTE. Nonetheless, the New York Times reports that GTE is “one of the most volatile issues in public education.” A leading analyst finds that “there is no issue in American education that is more fraught.”

Why is GTE so controversial? Why, despite strong support from parents and vigorous national and state advocacy movements, is progress lagging?

There are two huge obstacles. One is cost. The second is even more fundamental: It’s widespread criticism that GTE is inequitable and elitist; only a small percentage of students found eligible are Black, Latino or poor.

That makes it a political hot potato. Identification is pivotal, and requirements are being revised to replace subjective parent and teacher referrals with, as stated in Maryland’s model, “universal screening … and multiple indicators of potential.”

One dilemma is finding the right age for identification. A recent journal article concludes that giftedness is mobile: It can be influenced by nature or nurture. Policies vary. Maryland requires identification “as early as possible, but no later than Grade 3.”

Beyond identification, the lack of earmarked federal and state funds for GTE is a major barrier. The uncomfortable policy question is: Given very scarce funding for public schools, what priority should GTE get?

When I was a member of the Baltimore City school board in the early 2000s, there was an 8-1 vote to reallocate funds to gifted and talented students. I was the lone dissenter. I reasoned that – because city schools were extraordinarily underfunded and the overwhelming majority of students, predominantly Black and poor, weren’t coming close to meeting reading and math standards, we couldn’t afford the reallocation.

I think back on my vote uneasily. Highest priorities can’t be exclusive priorities. A balance must be struck between extra instruction for low-performing students and other valuable school programs, from art and music to career and technical education to GTE, and so on.

The leading national proponent of GTE is the Fordham Institute education think tank. Its president, Michael Petrilli (a policy star), has written  “How can we depolarize ‘gifted education’?” He points out the U.S. not only trails other countries in basic reading and math proficiency; we are far behind in “advanced” achievement. And his chief recommendations parallel the Maryland model.

But what’s actually happening on the ground? Data is limited but each local district does pretty much its own thing, subject to state guidance on best practices. Among the practices:  professional learning, enriched instruction, grouping, co-teaching, GTE specialists and self-contained classes.

A Hechinger Report in 2021 stated that Maryland’s 16% participation rate in GTE is highest in the nation. Still, Maryland reports that children living in poverty are the most underrepresented group in gifted and talented programs. Even the most committed GTE educators and advocates agree there’s a long way to go.

So now, should we come down on the side of more or less GTE? In a more moral nation, the problem would go away. There would be enough money to provide all students – from low-performing to gifted and talented – with an adequate, equitable education.

Of course that’s a cop-out. In the real world, the inescapable issue is whether the equity issues are so knotty that GTE, as some critics argue, should be abandoned altogether. I don’t think so.

Instead, even without more funding, GTE can be improved in various ways. For example, more data and evaluation of what’s working best. Another is to target scant money to what are called “talent development programs“ that seek to expand the number and racial balance of students qualifying for GTE.

Still, in the near future, I can’t support more funding because of the multiple competing needs. Advocates must, in the midst of the state’s fiscal crisis, set limited priorities.

For now, sorry to say, the best we can do is forcefully advocate for brighter prospects in the years ahead.
